I'm Commander Shepard, and this is my least favorite game on the Citadel.

This is a masters course in bad game design. All aspiring devs should play it as an example of what to avoid.

An absolute masterclass epic. 
What I can only assume was tireless work by the developers to create an intricate, believable universe at war with a looming threat, all with well thought out, realistic planets that feel as though you are reading a true-to-life encyclopedia, is nothing less than astonishing. This, coupled with at the very least decent and at the very best incredible and movingly written and acted dialogue and events creates a timeless achievement.
The core, squad based, largely set piece gameplay is weighty and feels realistic. It is incredibly satisfying and never tires in entertainment. The AI does a fine job, and tactical maneuvers and utilization of the powers and unit technologies system make for engaging gameplay.
As a whole this game is a vibing, humming, space fairing pocket plane that warps you into another reality in a satisfying, moving zen.

Because I've already reviewed Mass Effect Legendary Edition, I will avoid focusing on Mass Effect 3's storyline and single player campaign elements.  Needless to say, Mass Effect 3 is a spectacular science fiction RPG experience and I give it a perfect score, eclipsing all but the most masterclass of games.  Instead, I will focus on the much marginalized and maligned multiplayer game play mode.  I would also like to underscore that I have an additional 750 hours on Origin/EA Play and that my Steam hours do not summarize my experience with the game.  The Mass Effect 3 multiplayer mode is a fantastic game mode and is easily worth the 15-20 dollar sale price  alone, without even taking the 40-60 hour campaign into account.

Mass Effect 3 multiplayer operates as a 3rd person, objectives-based horde-mode cooperative survival game.  You control one of six classes: Adept (psychic), Soldier, Engineer, Sentinel (hybrid psychic), Infiltrator and Vanguard (close combat specialist).  Each class, in turn, has anywhere from 8-12 sub-classes.  The sub-classes can be built by leveling various skill trees, taking mutually exclusive abilities.  Do you want to focus on weapons?  What kind of weapons? Do you want to focus on powers?  Passive abilities?  Active abilities?  Do you want to be aggressive or defensive? Would you rather play support?  Are mobility, shields, health, melee, stealth important?  By leveling various skill trees within each sub-class, you can easily create 150-200 distinct playable character builds.  Builds vary wildly from sniping infiltrators, to blundering melee bruisers, to ingenious turret deploying engineers, grenade spamming sprinters, main line fighters, psychokinetic demigods and more.

Adding to this rich, complex depth, is Mass Effect 3's no less than 7 ammunition types, and over 75 different equipment modifications that you can use to add to various abilities.  More incredibly is that various ammunition types and powers can react with each other, creating explosive combinations.  Prime a target with one power and detonate them explosively with another.  Or, instead, detonate them with ammunition (or environmental hazards).  The amount of interaction is truly limitless.  Adding to this interactive freedom is no less than 5 major weapons classes including sniper rifles, assault rifles, sub machine guns, pistols and shotguns.  Each weapon class, in turn, has 10-15 different sub weapons that look, handle and behave completely differently.  Do you want the shield-stripping, close range Reegar shotgun?  The point-blank Claymore blunderbuss?  How about the long-range, armor penetrating Crusader shotgun?  Each weapon class has a variety of different sub-weapons that will ensure you can play to your preferred play style.

Weapons feel good, have punch and most are useful.  And it's in the game play, where Mass Effect 3 truly shines.  With an intuitive, smooth cover/mantling system, you can briskly maneuver through one of 10 different maps, while obliterating 4 different armies.  Enemy armies themselves all consist of 10 different units, with different aggressive proclivities, abilities and predilections.  Are they shielded?  Armored?  Fast or slow? What kind of powers/effects/ammunition are they vulnerable to?   Do they prefer distance or are they melee-focused?  Enemy armies not only behave differently but look and sound differently, providing important cues that can be provided to enhance decision-making.  Artificial intelligence scales throughout no less than 4 difficulty levels ranging from Bronze through Platinum.

Yes, some may criticize the game's use of one single button for mantling/cover/storm and others may lament that the game has an in-game currency but, ultimately, these are minor flaws in an extremely compelling horde mode experience.  Most interestingly is that the multiplayer mode actually contributes valuable points towards your single player campaign mission, reflecting an interesting prescience that most other similar games lack.  Bioware wants you to understand that your battle conducted by no-name heroes represent the desperate survival of various species during the apocalyptic Reaver invasion in Mass Effect 3.  It works.

All in all, Mass Effect 3 is a great multiplayer mode and if, you like Gears of War, Killing Floor or any other horde mode, you owe yourself the chance to try out this far superior and highly addictive alternative.

Highest possible recommendation.

I feel like the neutral review would be better but if I have to choose between two options we have, for the fact that the important things are either trash or nonexistant I have to go with negative, especially that often the trash EA app turns off and forces your game to also shutdown or it looses connection to internet and messes up your achivs and synchronization with cloud... even DA:O worked better than that app and it was written on papirus by blind egyptian...

Combat? pretty good and somehow engaging with most of the reloads being slightly different so it doesn't get boring too fast even if it can get frustrating at some point on the higher diffs... but which game doesn't have that?
Gameplay overall? beside some small issues (or sometimes larger) with rolling and sticking to walls/running next to them it's pretty much another Gears-like, that's all

Story? bland, boring, irrelevant for 99% of time as you just watch slow movie where you can choose to shake someones hand or say hello instead. Beside like 2-3 choices every other is just there so you can get the points for your playthrough or not even give you that and be there for the sake of being there. You are forced to play one character that will have the same issues regardless of any of your choices and will feel the same way about minor stuff even if [spoiler] you kill people left and right, like you can shoot to the back of a head of a innocent person whose mother just killed herself and still somehow feel bad about one random child or some other crap... at certain point making Shepard a human just doesn't make sense and her issues don't seem to match her deeds [/spoiler] and even if we skip over all that, whole game has literally just like 5 interesting moments and then it's ending, rest could be a cutscene that lasts 10h each time and I wouldn't even be mad at this point

Leveling up is simple again and that's cool, we still have some choice with the "evolutions" of skills, but they are pretty much not balanced and often it's same thing that just looks different for different classes
Again most of the cool mechanics from ME1 got forgotten and no lockpicking or any of that, planet scanning is way simplier than in ME2 but it also has less meaning so that's ok, side activities are just for the dlc and they get unlocked pretty late, but it's casino so it's worth it and companion stuff also is handled in a decent way where for the most important stuff you will be messaged by them so you just need to check on the computer for the bare minimum and no secret interactions like [spoiler] Tali and Garrus kissing (?) [/spoiler]
Weapons, their upgrades and mods are again fun... but nothing equals to ME1 with how stupidly broken some of them were and how cool it was to experiment around for some nice combos

At the end it looks like it's a good game but only if you are not here for the RPG aspect of it, tbh if it wouldn't be for the achivs I would most likely just stop halfway through and read the quests, their outcomes and all about endings on the wiki and it would be a better experience.

Good that I have dementia so I can hope to forget how bland this game was and try to keep only the memory of the ending

Oh and multiplayer is kinda fun but when you have no weapons or better characters it's annoying how much you get carried by people who have hundreds of levels, but that's also kinda the issue with older games and mp so it's not an issue or at least not their fault

I'd give it 6, maybe 7 if I would spend more time in casino and it had some interesting missions or anything extra but if we are giving extra points we would need to take away extra for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ app so 6 feels like a good pick regardless of that
Good, but could be better. There could be a ending like the ME2 ending, not 'select option 1,2 or 3' kind of ending.

Just a quick review of whether or not you can actually start the game or not:

I did just get the game (to complete my collection of all Mass Effect Games) and at first it asked me to insert a product key. After that i closed that screen and started the game again (i did it through the EA Play store, for me it automatically got added to my EA Play library) and after that it worked without asking me to insert any product key (it also starts fine if i start it through steam now, so not sure if starting it through EA Play made any difference).
